documents.abstract: As the intelligence of an AI agent increases relative to a trusted monitor, so does the risk that the monitor will fail to understand the agent's actions or to evaluate them confidently. We introduce interrogation protocols to a high-stakes AI control setting, and allow the monitor to ask the untrusted agent questions about confusing actions. For interrogation to improve safety, a weaker model must be able to distinguish misleading explanations produced by an attack policy from genuine ones produced by an honest policy. We find that on a held-out subset of BashArena, an interrogation protocol improves safety at a 1% audit budget from 72.6% for an actions-only baseline, which does not use interrogations, to 79.5% (+7.0 pp [+0.9, +20.1], 95% paired bootstrap interval), but most of this uplift can be captured by having a trusted model state a specific concern. More broadly, our work suggests that interrogating agents can improve safety, allowing monitors to catch more attacks at a larger capability gap.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI has ended the assumption that unsupervised student work reflects a student’s own unaided thinking, forcing a return to first principles in assessment. This article uses The University of Sydney’s two-lane approach, which separates secure assessment of learning from open assessment for and as learning, to frame a practical account of putting AI into students’ hands. Drawing on ‘Dr MattTabolism’, an AI biochemistry tutor I built and deployed, and on a computational study of how students actually used it, I show a consistent gap between how such tools are designed and how they are used. Students largely sought answers rather than sustained dialogue, satisfaction did not correlate with improved learning outcomes, and usage concentrated around deadlines. How educators contextualised AI use affected learning more than how the tool behaved. I argue that this offloading is partly a product of over-assessment, and that formative, lower-stakes work remains essential precisely because it is where students can afford the desirable difficulties that learning requires. Reducing assessment load is a validity measure, not a soft option. I close with practical starting points for educators, framed around the pedagogical roles AI can play and the risks each carries, and the educator’s role as designer.

The promise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education has motivated a rapidly growing literature whose titles, abstracts, and keywords mention acceptance, attitudes, intention, or perception more than six times as often as self-regulated learning or metacognition. This critical review argues that research on GenAI in education is repeating the founding mistake of learning analytics, measuring what is easy to count rather than what matters for learning. Building on the COPES model of self-regulated learning, this paper develops the gradual reduction of AI delegation (GRAD) framework, in which GenAI performs, proposes, or prompts at eight task stages. Within GRAD, GenAI can take on operations essential to the learning goal. Such delegation helps rather than replaces learning only when the support fades as learners improve. For claims that GenAI improves learning, the paper proposes four validity criteria, namely unassisted outcomes, process evidence, calibration, and ideally gains that outlast the support.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: As human-driven vehicles (HVs) and automated vehicles (AVs) increasingly share public roads, AVs must anticipate how human drivers negotiate right-of-way conflicts. Using 648 simulator trials across 6 competitive HV–AV scenarios, we apply maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning to recover scenario-specific reward structures representing efficiency, safety, and comfort. We then train a lightweight hybrid Markov decision process policy through behavior cloning followed by reward-based fine-tuning. The hybrid model achieves lower average displacement error than behavior-cloning-only and reinforcement-learning-only baselines across all scenario groups. A separate outcome head predicts whether the human-driven vehicle or AV will proceed first from partial trajectories. Participant characteristics are incorporated only through post-hoc calibration of the outcome-prediction threshold, while reward and control-policy learning remain scenario-level. Accuracy, F1, and AUC improve as more interaction context becomes available, and participant-aware calibration provides modest early prediction benefits in scenarios where the interaction state is sufficiently informative.

A Large Language Model (LLM), its harness, and the test-time compute budget jointly determine its behavior. Consequently, the same underlying model, embedded in different agentic workflows or allocated different amounts of test-time compute, can exhibit markedly different performance. Psychologists face an analogous challenge when evaluating human performance: the same person may behave differently under different incentives and levels of deliberation. Psychological tasks therefore provide an ideal testbed for studying such behavioral variation. However, when adapted to LLMs, these tasks are typically text-transcribed, replaying fixed, language-rendered experiments as static prompts. This format is ill-suited to agent evaluation, where actions can alter future observations and task states. Conversely, although dynamic environments are prevalent in the evaluation of LLM agents, they rarely ask whether the resulting behavior is human-like. Here, we bridge this gap by transforming psychological tasks into dynamic environments in which agents can interact and by using a learned human-policy model to evaluate how compatible the resulting behavioral trajectories are with human behavior. Across these environments, we find that this compatibility varies with an LLM's agentic configuration and the psychological task, and that memory raises it mainly by making choices more predictable rather than more human-like. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation of LLM agents in psychology-inspired environments, accounting for both the backbone model and its agentic scaffold.

Introduction Job motivation among university professors is a key factor in the quality of higher education, especially in basic sciences within health sciences programs. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) analyzes motivation on a continuum from demotivation and extrinsic motivation to intrinsic motivation. The objective of this study is to explore the job motivation of basic science professors at a private university in Santiago during the year 2025, based on SDT. Materials and methods Exploratory, cross-sectional, pilot quantitative study. The sample consisted of basic science teachers in health sciences programs. Job motivation was assessed using the Multidimensional Work Motivation Scale (MWMS). Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, considering comparisons by sex, age range, and years of teaching experience. Results The motivational profile was predominantly autonomous, characterized by high levels of intrinsic motivation and identified self-regulation. Low levels of demotivation were observed. Women showed higher levels of autonomous motivation compared to men. Older teachers showed greater autonomous motivation. A statistically significant correlation was found between years of teaching experience, identified self-regulation, and intrinsic motivation. Conclusion Autonomous motivation predominates among basic science teachers, with teaching experience being a key factor. This study provides relevant evidence for the design of institutional strategies.

Background: Germany's healthcare system is often described as lagging behind internationally in terms of digital transformation. While academic and health policy debates mainly focus on structural and organizational challenges, human factors have received less attention. However, Motivation and volition may be important for the adoption and use of digital technologies. Therefore, this scoping review examined the current state of research on the motivation of healthcare professionals in Germany to engage with digital technologies. Methods: A literature review was conducted using a broad search strategy in PubMed, APA PsycInfo, and FIS Bildung in February 2026. The search strategy followed the PCC framework. The population of interest comprised physicians, nurses, and other health professionals. The concepts investigated included motivation, volition, engagement, and incentive systems in the context of the digitalization of the German healthcare system. German- and English-language publications from the previous ten years were included. The identified studies were screened according to predefined eligibility criteria, and the findings were synthesized narratively. Results: The included studies identify motivation as a relevant influencing factor, although it is rarely conceptualized in depth. Research mainly focuses on political and financial incentives as well as learning-related approaches such as gamification and interactive interfaces. Intrinsic motivation is addressed mostly indirectly, particularly regarding self-motivation, openness to change, and patient interaction. Uncertainties surrounding health data and digital applications are described as barriers that may reduce willingness to use digital technologies. Conclusion: The findings highlight the need for theory-informed and profession-specific research, with greater attention to intrinsic motivation and its interaction with structural conditions.

China’s government is making artificial intelligence (AI) a national development priority and is promoting its adoption across the country’s economy and society. This essay discusses how AI may affect China’s economy, specifically how it may challenge the performance-based legitimacy China’s government has depended upon over the last several decades. In particular, this essay shows how AI affects workers in different industries, workers at different stages of their careers, different age groups, and different geographic locations. Evidence suggests AI is driving down demand for routine tasks and certain forms of creative work and that wealthier, more economically diversified regions are better able to cope with the disruption. It also shows that feelings of insecurity are on the rise, as demand for entry-level workers may be decreasing and senior workers now confront a situation in which their junior counterparts can do some of their jobs. This essay also discusses opportunities arising from AI in the public sector, specifically how AI could help China’s economy by creating new industries and raising productivity and can help its government by improving the delivery of public services. Finally, this essay discusses how China’s government is trying to help people who have been directly and indirectly affected by AI through initiatives like employment programs, court rulings protecting employees, and monitoring of how the economic gains from AI are distributed. Although the evidence shows AI results in these labor market changes, whether they will undermine public trust remains a projection rather than an established fact.

documents.abstract: Online reviews aggregate millions of individual judgments into signals that shape where people eat, stay and travel to, and increasingly read them as evidence of the reputation of places. Nevertheless, whether such reputations really reflect the places or more the instruments used to measure them is unclear. Here we compare two instruments for measuring trust and bias in 100,000 Yelp reviews from ten US cities: a large language model based agentic system including an evaluator critic loop, and a corpus-based tool built on pretrained classifiers, lexicons and rule-based features. Our results show that the two instruments agree on credibility, but not at all on plausibility. They also respond to different use of words and phrases. The corpus-based better flagged complaints and generalizations, whereas the agent better quoted references to social groups. We also found that with five examples, the agent treats ordinary superlatives as bias far more often than with none or one. Aggregated to cities, both instruments find little variation as less than half a percent of the variance of review level reputation lies between cities. This small differences between cities mostly arise from different levels of trust (in case of the agentic tool) and from bias (in case of the corpus-based tool), and the two instruments rank the cities differently. Reputation derived from platform reviews therefore depends on how the reviews are processed and analyzed. As platforms delegate this to language models, the definitions and examples built into these models become part of how places are valued.

documents.abstract: Communication devices generate an unprecedented potential for interconnection, transcending social interaction across time and distance, and create both undoubted benefits and new challenges. This dynamic requires updating how we study and intervene to promote coexistence. The background research for this paper involved an exhaustive literature review and an empirical 600-participant sample study. It yielded three outcomes: (I) The conversion of coexistence and perception of otherness from concepts into objective variables; (II) A scale’s design and validation for measuring otherness as an objective variable; (III) A serious game virtual platform. Thus, reporting this platform is the main objective of the current paper. The findings show it is possible, in a virtual serious game environment, to use the incidence of coexistence on the perception of otherness to manipulate the former as a variable. It can generate positive effects in promoting social cohesion, together with narrative persuasion mediation and an avatar’s personification.

Technological developments in the Industrial Revolution 4.0 era have encouraged Filadelfia to continue innovating in its promotional activities. One of the efforts undertaken is through the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Instagram content as a means of communication and promotion. This study aims to: 1) examine the use of AI in Instagram content among followers of the @filadelfiasushii Instagram account, 2) assess prospective consumers’ trust among followers of the @filadelfiasushii Instagram account, and 3) measure the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in @filadelfiasushii Instagram content on prospective consumers’ trust. The theories employed include Artificial Intelligence, encompassing the dimensions of AI Awareness, Perceived Quality, Perceived Authenticity, and Transparency, as well as the theory of Prospective Consumer Trust, encompassing Credibility, Benevolence, Integrity, and Purchase Intention. Using a quantitative approach with a survey method, the study population comprised 152 followers of the @filadelfiasushii Instagram account, with a sample of 110 respondents. The data analysis technique used was simple linear regression. The results indicate that: 1) the use of AI in @filadelfiasushii Instagram content is in the high category with an average score of 3.89, 2) prospective consumers’ trust is in the high category with an average score of 3.95, and 3) the use of AI in @filadelfiasushii Instagram content has a significant influence on prospective consumers’ trust, with an R Square value of 0.683 or 68.3%, while the remaining 31.7% is influenced by other factors.

Indonesia has written artificial intelligence (AI) into national education policy within six years, yet few studies ask what problem these documents say AI solves. This article asks which problems four national policy documents represent when they address AI in education, and what they leave unexamined. I analyzed a national AI strategy (2020), a ministerial circular on AI ethics (2023), a university guide to generative AI (2024), and a joint decree of seven ministers on digital technology and AI in education (2026). Using Bacchi's “What's the problem represented to be?” (WPR) approach and the theory of sociotechnical imaginaries, I coded 20 excerpts and kept representations that recur in at least two documents. Four met that rule: education supplies AI talent, AI use is an ethics and integrity issue, readiness is a learner trait, and local culture is content or value. Together they place the work of readiness on students and teachers. The coded excerpts do not say who pays for that work, and they treat local knowledge as material to retrieve and not as a design input. Indonesian scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022 sit well below the average of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which makes that silence matter. With one analyst and a small corpus, the study describes patterns, not effects. Policy writers can name the body that bears the cost of readiness, tie AI literacy to foundational skills, and give holders of local knowledge a role in design.
keywords: What's the problem represented to be

documents.abstract: With the increasing prevalence of artificial intelligence (AI) in daily life, it is essential for young people to be proficient in communicating with AI systems. This research paper introduces a game-based tool named Promptémon for middle schoolers, designed to teach prompt engineering: phrasing instructions so an AI gives a useful answer. It uses a creature-battle game format where players create prompts to defeat AI opponents. Players combine prepared instructions with ''modifier chips'' that represent personas, styles, or audiences. The game gives immediate feedback, using a second AI step to check whether the response meets the challenge. The research questions were: (RQ1) How do middle school students' confidence and self-reported understanding of prompt engineering compare before and after playing? and (RQ2) How do students respond to the game's features for trying and refining prompts? Promptémon was tested with students in grades 6 to 8 (60 forms before, 60 after) at a public school AI event in a Texas city, in visits of about seven to ten minutes. Self-reported confidence (4 or 5 of 5) rose from 48.3% to 78.3% (29 to 47 of 60). Of 53 matched students, 26 rated themselves higher, 8 lower, and 19 the same (sign test, p = .0059). After play, 44 of 60 agreed the feedback helped them understand how to improve, while 28 of 60 wanted to try other chip combinations. However, choice of the most structured prompt did not rise (31, then 27 of 52, p = .22), and only 5 of 60 named a prompt component in their own words. Because all outcomes are self-reports from one short session with no comparison group, these results describe immediate reactions, not gains in prompting skill. This study presents a game-based way to show young learners the parts of a prompt.

Assessments of responsible artificial intelligence (AI) use in engineering design usually focus on properties of the system, such as accuracy, reliability, transparency, bias and human oversight. The task given to the system (its objective, requirements, constraints and evaluation criteria) results from earlier choices that correct system operation cannot justify. Based on a critical-comparative analysis of the literature on AI ethics, design theory and requirements engineering, we distinguish the assessment of solution correctness from the assessment of the adequacy of problem formulation. In our coding, frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF, IEEE 7000, Value Sensitive Design and requirements validation cover this stage only partially. We identify three roles of AI in the design process: solver, evaluator and co-author of the task. The latter two act while the task is still being formed. We propose the Problem Formulation Assessment (PFA), a conceptual model with seven dimensions, including the validity of proxy measures, stakeholder representation and AI involvement in task formulation; only the last has no counterpart in the frameworks examined. The model is illustrated with generative space planning, a multi-agent specification system, passive vehicle safety tests and a hypothetical footbridge project. It has not been empirically validated, and we outline a validation agenda.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has triggered an institutional crisis of academic trust. This challenge is characterized by an "adoption-trust paradox," where ubiquitous student usage coexists with deep ethical skepticism and concerns over academic integrity. While existing research predominantly focuses on individual technology acceptance models (e.g., TAM, UTAUT), this study shifts the analytical lens to institutional governance and its marketing implications, framing academic trust as a vital strategic brand asset that drives organizational legitimacy and student behavioral intentions. We propose and empirically test a multidimensional governance framework consisting of four core pillars: ethical transparency, algorithmic accountability, digital AI literacy, and adaptive AI governance. Utilizing a quantitative research design and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), we analyze survey data from 380 higher education students in Tunisia. The structural model reveals that Adaptive AI Governance is the most powerful predictor of Institutional Trust (β = 0.297, p < 0.001), followed by Algorithmic Accountability (β = 0.258, p < 0.001) and Ethical Transparency (β = 0.231, p < 0.001), while AI Literacy has a smaller but significant effect (β = 0.137, p = 0.006). Institutional Trust, in turn, exhibits an exceptionally strong positive relationship with Perceived Institutional Ethicality (β = 0.741, p < 0.001). Together, trust and ethicality explain 61.2% of the variance in students' behavioral intentions toward sustainable AI use, with perceived ethicality acting as a significant partial mediating mechanism (β_indirect = 0.337, p < 0.001). Beyond pedagogical compliance, these findings demonstrate that robust governance directly enhances institutional brand equity, student attraction, and procedural legitimacy. We outline strategic recommendations for university marketers and educators to co-create proactive, values-led learning ecosystems that strengthen academic reputation in the digital era.

documents.abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent adapts to what it observes, so a strategy that keeps winning in practice may already have stopped working by the time it is used. Motivated by these settings, we study a player who tries strategies in practice games against an adaptive opponent, decides when to stop, and then either selects one strategy for the next game or abstains. The goal is to select a strategy that meets a target win probability while rarely selecting one that has already fallen below it. For a single strategy, we propose the Sequential Private Accumulated-excess Rule (SPAR), which accumulates evidence through a capped likelihood ratio and selects the strategy once this evidence reaches a privately drawn uniform threshold. We show that the stopping time must involve such private randomness. The number of games SPAR needs is inversely proportional to the error tolerance, and this rate is optimal even when the opponent happens not to adapt. To select among multiple strategies, we introduce Screen-then-SPAR, which screens candidates in stages before applying SPAR. The procedure adapts to the best strategy's unknown initial margin above the target and achieves the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. The performance of Screen-then-SPAR is demonstrated through simulations and two real-data studies, one using recorded coding-agent attacks from MonitoringBench and the other using rock-paper-scissors matches between human players and an adaptive bot.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in complex decision-making tasks across various domains. However, trust mis-calibration in AI, manifested as either over-trust or under-trust, remains a significant challenge, impacting human-AI collaboration and decision quality. This paper investigates factors influencing trust mis-calibration in AI through a user study on a speech-based deception detection task, an inherently complex and ambiguous domain. It examines (1) the relationship between user performance and trust calibration; (2) the role of local explanations (i.e., linguistic and acoustic features of deceptive speech) in shaping trust calibration; and (3) the influence of case-specific cues on trust calibration. In a study involving 52 participants, findings suggest that high-performing users exhibit significantly lower under-trust, but do not differ in over-trust compared to low-performing users. Analysis of local explanations reveals that under-trust occurs when linguistic and acoustic features misalign with deception outcomes. On the other side, over-trust arises when these features align with deception but the AI’s decision does not, suggesting that over-trust follows less rational decision-making patterns. Furthermore, users rely on different cues depending on their trust calibration: under-trusting users focus on speech features, over-trusting users rely on general perception, and properly calibrated users incorporate social, cultural, and emotional cues. These findings underscore the need for AI systems to tailor explanations based on user expertise and develop cognitive strategies to mitigate trust mis-calibration and foster effective human-AI collaboration.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Online platforms provide learners of English as a foreign language (EFL) with access to stories and poems for independent listening practice. Evidence on how learners experience anxiety and motivation when using these materials remains limited. This study examined listening anxiety, motivation, and preferences for stories and poems across three platforms: British Council, Light Up Your Brain, and Children’s Poetry Archive. The descriptive quantitative survey involved 32 purposively selected students in the English Department at Universitas Negeri Padang who had completed the Basic Listening course and used all three platforms. A validated four-point Likert-scale questionnaire assessed cognitive, affective, and behavioral anxiety, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, preferences for stories or poems, and experiences with the platforms. Responses were summarized using frequencies, percentages, and means. Mean scores indicated high cognitive anxiety (2.64) and affective anxiety (2.50) alongside high intrinsic motivation (2.93) and extrinsic motivation (3.04). The low mean for behavioral anxiety (2.26) suggested that students seldom avoided or abandoned listening tasks. Students preferred stories and found them easier to follow because of their clear plots. They valued poetry for its rhythm and expressive delivery and reported that replaying audio on the British Council platform helped ease anxiety. The findings suggest that educators can support autonomous listening by introducing stories before poetry and guiding students in the strategic use of playback controls.

Introduction Generative social robots (GSRs) powered by large language models offer new possibilities for personalized tutoring in higher education, but also introduce risks related to misinformation, missing transparency, or reinforcing incorrect student responses. Prior work identified knowledge-based design (KBD) requirements that define the information GSRs need to tutor responsibly and effectively in higher education. Methods In this paper, we operationalized selected KBD requirements in the Reachy Mini robot platform through system prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and stateful prompt orchestration. We present Teachy Mini, a GSR tutoring prototype based on these design requirements. To test the system, we conducted a preliminary evaluation study. Participants (N = 24) completed a robot-guided learning session about research methodologies. They learned with either Teachy Mini or a robot without the KBD features. Results and discussion Teachy Mini was perceived as significantly more aligned with responsible tutoring behavior than the robot in the control condition. In addition, a qualitative analysis showed that Teachy Mini more often used context-sensitive explanations, Socratic questions, and personalized feedback compared to the robot without KBD features. No significant between-condition differences were found in system acceptance, intrinsic motivation, or learning effectiveness, although exploratory analyses suggested a positive effect of KBD on objective learning gains when accounting for learner preferences. Furthermore, an exploratory path model suggested that the robot’s perceived responsible behavior may be associated with learner motivation and acceptance. Overall, the study suggests that KBD can meaningfully shape responsible robot tutoring behavior. However, the effect of KBD on learner experiences requires further research.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The leading developers of artificial intelligence (AI) are among the most valuable and influential companies in the world, yet their corporate governance has received little attention in the literature on AI governance. We contribute to filling this gap by comparing the governance of four leading AI firms (OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Alphabet/Google) and, more briefly, Mistral, Meta and DeepSeek. Two observations stand out. First, the leading AI firms are all closely held or controlled through dual-class shares, which reflects a broader revival of founder control in tech firms. Second, the firms differ sharply in whether and how their stated purpose is protected. OpenAI is controlled by a nonprofit foundation, Anthropic by founders under a purpose trust with the right to elect a majority of the board, Alphabet by founders with conventional checks and balances, and SpaceX by a single founder with few checks. Purpose-protecting devices-public benefit corporation status, foundation control and purpose trusts-are imperfect and must cope with enormous challenges, but from a governance perspective they are a great deal better than complete autarchy (non-governance). The paper concludes that private-law governance arrangements can be a valuable complement to public regulation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates educational documentation, workplace management, clinical screening, and other institutional processes that affect neurodivergent people. This article argues that prevailing approaches to AI governance, disability rights, and cognitive liberty may fail to make visible a category of harm that is structural, cumulative, and experienced through persistent misrecognition rather than a single identifiable adverse event. I call this problem the Invisible Harm Doctrine. Drawing on scholarship on autistic camouflaging, autistic burnout, sensory and perceptual difference, algorithmic management, automation bias, AI fairness, and emerging neurorights, the article develops a normative account of how apparently neutral AI-mediated systems may reproduce neurotypical assumptions about communication, attention, behavior, and performance. It draws on Epistemic Parallax, a construct developed in the author’s prior published work, as a conceptual account of the mismatch between the normative frames through which systems classify behavior and the lived contexts those classifications purport to assess. The article proposes neurodivergent cognitive liberty as a complementary normative formulation, not an existing legal right and not a replacement for present neurorights frameworks. It states the principal objections to the doctrine and responds to them, and it concludes by identifying research, design, and governance questions necessary to evaluate whether and how these harms can be detected, challenged, and mitigated. The article does not report new primary data, establish clinical efficacy, or propose a ready-to-adopt legal standard.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Sewing workers in the informal sector are potentially susceptible to work-related stress due to job demands that require precision, high levels of concentration, and the completion of tasks according to specific targets. Individual characteristics are thought to influence a worker's ability to cope with pressure while on the job. This study aimed to identify the relationship between work-related stress and individual characteristics—specifically age, education level, and length of service—among sewing workers in Karanganyar Village, Tirto District, Pekalongan Regency. The study employed a descriptive-analytic, cross-sectional design. A purposive sampling method was used to select 31 respondents. The Job Stress Scale (JSS) questionnaire was utilized to measure the work-related stress variable. Data were analyzed using univariate and bivariate methods, applying the Chi-Square test or Fisher’s Exact Test with a significance level of 0.05. A total of 25 respondents (80.6%) experienced work-related stress. The analysis indicated that age (p=0.083; OR=7.50; 95% CI: 0.76–74.16) and length of service (p=0.363; OR=3.93; 95% CI: 0.40–38.71) were not significantly associated with work-related stress. Conversely, a significant relationship was found between education level and work-related stress (p<0.001; OR=120.00; 95% CI: 6.38–2,257.57). Workers with lower levels of education experienced higher levels of work-related stress compared to those with higher levels of education. There is a need for education on stress management and the improvement of occupational health to support the mental well-being of sewing workers.

warm-up activities represent an important component of effective English language teaching. Although they are traditionally used to introduce a lesson and attract students' attention, their pedagogical potential extends far beyond these functions. This article examines the role of warm-up activities in enhancing students' engagement, critical thinking, creativity, spontaneous communication, and classroom interaction. The study is based on the author's practical teaching experience in a school environment, where warm-up activities are systematically incorporated into every English lesson. Six techniques are examined: associative thinking through the Rule of Three, the Yes-or-No Challenge, the Draw and Guess activity, the Tic-Tac-Toe game, crossword challenges, and charades. Particular attention is paid to students' ability to produce original responses, express opinions, interpret visual information, demonstrate humour, and participate actively in classroom communication. Regular classroom observations suggest that these activities help students become involved in lessons more quickly and create opportunities for meaningful language practice and cognitive engagement. The article argues that warm-up activities should be considered not merely introductory exercises but purposeful pedagogical tools that integrate language development with critical and creative thinking.

Usability testing depends on people, and people's time does not speed up at the pace that software production demands. Large language models (LLMs) now promise to remove people from testing by generating simulated users that browse websites, answer questionnaires and give interviews. This paper examines how academic research understands that promise. It combines a critical literature review with a genealogical reading that follows the simulated user from the cognitive models of the 1980s to current generative agents. The paper makes four claims. First, testing without the user is an old aim of human-computer interaction (HCI), and cost has always justified it. Second, the validity criterion for user models shifted from predictive precision to believability, and recent studies that return to precision report weak results. Third, simulated participants conflict with the values of academic research and with methods that treat participation as a political right, with Participatory Design as the limit case. Fourth, the Latin American literature found in this review uses generative AI to support expert inspection and contains no study of synthetic users. That gap leaves open questions about who gets represented and about research ethics regulation in Brazil. The paper closes with an agenda of open problems. As part of its method, it reports that the review itself used an LLM as research assistant, and it discusses what that implies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The deep integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has attracted sustained attention from educational researchers and practitioners concerning how such tools reshape student learning. Scholars have yet to agree on whether—and, more importantly, under what conditions—GenAI facilitates or inhibits learning. This disagreement persists in part because most researchers conceptualize GenAI use as a single, undifferentiated exposure. Prior scholarship rests on linear assumptions and fails to account for why, at a given level of GenAI dependence, different layers of higher-order thinking respond asymmetrically. Drawing on the too-much-of-a-good-thing (TMGT) metatheory, the expertise reversal effect (ERE) as an interpretive framework—whose implications we test but whose underlying mechanism we do not measure—and Bloom’s revised taxonomy, we hypothesize that GenAI dependence and higher-order thinking ability exhibit an inverted U-shaped relationship. Given that learners’ capacity to steer GenAI outputs shapes the benefits and risks of GenAI reliance, prompt engineering competence (PEC) is modeled as a metacognitive calibration mechanism moderating this curvilinear relationship. Based on 713 valid questionnaires collected from three universities located in the eastern, central, and western regions of China, hierarchical regression and the Sasabuchi–Lind–Mehlum (SLM) formal test confirmed a significant inverted U-shape; students with higher PEC exhibited a rightward-shifted turning point and a flatter descending segment. Robustness checks based on Winsorization and 1000-run permutation tests indicated that the main inverted-U effect remained stable, whereas the curvilinear moderation by PEC received more tentative support. Theoretically, we extend TMGT from psychology and management into human–AI cognitive coupling; practically, we offer tentative guidance for setting pedagogical boundaries of GenAI integration and for stratified cultivation of prompt engineering literacy.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. As AI also makes decisions about work allocation, we compare a set of LLMs. We find many models also deviate from purely objective decisions, particularly when the project stakes are low, but there is wide heterogeneity as to how much and in what manner they weigh enjoyment. These results raise questions about what role human experience may play in decisions around where and how to integrate AI into workplaces. Integration may be jagged across settings due to consideration not only of the relative capabilities of workers, but also the human experience of work, the valence of that experience (e.g., more strongly weighing aversion), the context (e.g., stakes), and who is making or guiding such choices (human or LLM).

With the growing demand for ESG disclosure and evaluation, constructing high-quality datasets for automatically extracting ESG-related information from large-scale documents has become essential. However, ESG annotation remains challenging due to strong context dependence, ambiguous label boundaries, and the need for domain expertise, resulting in high annotation cost and limited scalability. To address these challenges, we propose TRAE (TRustworthy Automated ESG annotation), a multi-agent framework for scalable and reliable ESG data construction. Unlike direct LLM-based annotation, TRAE evaluates annotation reliability by modeling agreement, confidence, and reasoning consistency among multiple agents through a structured multi-step reasoning process. Experimental results demonstrate that TRAE improves annotation performance compared with existing automated annotation strategies. Furthermore, TRAE supports a hybrid human-AI annotation strategy that assigns expert labeling only to uncertain samples, reducing annotation cost while preserving data quality. Using TRAE, we construct a high-quality ESG dataset containing approximately 20,000 instances with complete reasoning traces, intermediate agent outputs, and reliability information to enhance transparency and reproducibility. Overall, this work provides a practical and scalable framework for trustworthy ESG data construction. The code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/nowzer0/TRAE.

La transformación digital y la inteligencia artificial (IA) han modificado las condiciones en que la gerencia obtiene información, evalúa alternativas y asume responsabilidad por sus decisiones. El objetivo de este artículo fue analizar cómo ambos procesos reconfiguran la toma de decisiones gerenciales, con énfasis en las empresas de América Latina. Se desarrolló una revisión documental sistematizada, de enfoque cualitativo y alcance descriptivo-interpretativo, sobre un corpus de 31 artículos científicos con identificador digital verificado, publicados entre 2018 y 2026 más un referente clásico, de los cuales 17 corresponden a autores e instituciones iberoamericanas. El análisis de contenido se organizó en cuatro ejes: la transformación digital como condición habilitante, las configuraciones de decisión entre personas y algoritmos, la evidencia empírica latinoamericana y los riesgos y capacidades gerenciales asociados. Los resultados indican que la IA aporta valor decisorio cuando se integra en procesos administrativos concretos y cuando la organización dispone de datos, talento y estructuras adecuadas; que la literatura converge en un modelo de complementariedad, donde el algoritmo procesa complejidad y el directivo resuelve ambigüedad; y que en la región persiste una brecha entre la digitalización comercial y el uso analítico de los datos. Se concluye que la calidad de la decisión gerencial asistida por IA depende menos de la tecnología adquirida que de la madurez digital, la gobernanza de datos y el criterio directivo.

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) has significantly transformed how organizations manage information, develop strategic alternatives, and support managerial decision-making, shifting leadership responsibilities from information gathering toward directing, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated outputs. This transformation raises critical questions concerning the boundaries of human and machine authority, accountability for AI-assisted decisions, and the strategic capabilities required for responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the transformation of managerial leadership in AI-assisted decision-making, identify key dimensions of managerial accountability, and synthesize the strategic capabilities necessary for responsible technology integration. A qualitative approach employing an integrative literature review was adopted, drawing on peer-reviewed journal articles, academic books, and official documents published primarily between 2020 and 2026. The selected literature was analyzed through thematic coding and critical comparative analysis. The findings indicated that managerial leadership evolved around three interrelated functions: directing, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated outputs, rather than simply experiencing a reduction in responsibilities through automation. Managerial accountability encompassed four dimensions: clear allocation of responsibility, transparency and traceability, meaningful human oversight, and risk management. These dimensions provided a conceptual basis for maintaining human accountability in AI-assisted decision-making. Furthermore, five strategic capabilities were identified as central to responsible AI integration: AI literacy, knowledge integration, governance capabilities, strategic adaptability, and organizational learning. The study concluded that managerial leadership transformation in the era of generative AI depended not merely on technological adoption but also on the integration of human judgment, robust accountability mechanisms, and adaptive strategic capabilities. These findings contributed to a conceptual framework for responsible AI governance and sustainable organizational adaptation.

documents.abstract: Person-centred methods have been used in workplace bullying literature to identify different target groups. In this study, we use these methods to determine whether target groups are identifiable based on whether people experience face-to-face or cyberbullying behaviours. Using data collected from a sample of 748 employees at two time points separated by six months, we find that bullying targets seem to experience face-to-face and cyber acts concurrently, rather than separately. Indeed, latent profile analysis shows three categories of victimhood: “No Bullying”, “Infrequent Bullying”, and “Regular Bullying”. We then explore predictors of profile membership, finding that role conflict was significantly associated with membership of the “Infrequent” and “Regular” profiles both cross-sectionally and over time. In contrast, role clarity only showed cross-sectional associations with membership of the Infrequent Bullying profile. In a final set of analyses, we investigate whether latent changes in role stressors influence transitions of people across profiles over time. We find that role clarity changes were linked to transitions between the “No Bullying” and “Infrequent Bullying” profiles, whereas role conflict change was associated with movement between the “Regular Bullying” and “Infrequent Bullying” profiles. These findings imply that enhancing role clarity may prevent bullying, whereas reducing role conflict may de-escalate bullying.

Electric micromobility (e-mobility) has expanded rapidly, accompanied by growing public concern regarding risky behaviours, deaths and injuries, particularly among young people. This study provides the first systematic empirical characterisation of Australia’s e-mobility culture among young riders through a comparative observational analysis of 400 TikTok videos featuring e-bikes and e-scooters. Videos were systematically coded for rider characteristics, riding environments, technical performance, risky behaviours, vehicle modifications, symbolic expressions, audience engagement, and associated textual content. Male riders dominated both communities, particularly e-bike content, where their presence was almost exclusive. Conversion kits, custom builds and high-powered vehicles were prominent features of e-bike content, with Surron overwhelmingly dominating brand references, whereas e-scooter content featured a wider range of commercial brands, led by Xiaomi. Creators voluntarily showcased high motor wattages and speed readings, often indicating capabilities well beyond those permitted for conventional e-mobility devices. Wheelies and burnouts were considerably more common in e-bike videos, whereas e-scooter content more frequently featured throttle testing and speed demonstrations. Helmet use was almost universal in applicable e-bike videos but observed in only around half of e-scooter videos. E-bike content also exhibited a more pronounced culture of defiance, with substantially more references to profanity, violence and gangs, alongside recurring narratives involving police pursuit and evasion. Hip-hop predominated more strongly in e-bike content, whereas electronic music was more common in e-scooter videos. References to parents also appeared in creators’ narratives, often concerning permission, warnings or reassurance. Explicit numerical speed displays were consistently associated with greater audience engagement after accounting for creator popularity. The study establishes an empirical foundation for understanding the online dimensions of contemporary e-mobility and highlights the importance of incorporating digital culture into future public safety research and interventions.

Coding agents (CAs) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. As these CAs take up more tasks and responsibilities, it is imperative for software engineers to understand the CA's rationale behind its' decisions, also known as the chain-of-thought (CoT). During the interaction, some CAs are capable of showing this CoT as a separate message to users with the goal of providing transparency and explainability. However, its effectiveness as an explainable AI (XAI) mechanism for end-users in software engineering has not yet been established in the literature. This motivates us to understand their experiences with the CoT message as an XAI tool through a survey and semi-structured follow-up interviews with 36 software engineers. Through thematic analysis of the survey responses and interview transcripts, we found that CoT message is an indispensable tool for software engineers in terms of transparency, scrutability, and trust towards the CA. However, various instances of CoT messages being overly verbose, containing technical information that does not match the users' expertise, or being perceived by the users as ``detached'' from the conversation because the ``agent is talking to itself'', lead to comprehension difficulties and selective use or abandonment of the tool. We synthesize these insights to inform the design of CoT messages that support software engineers in their explainability needs.

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative AI is increasingly proposed to support spatial planning, yet empirical evidence on how such systems perform in realistic planning workflows and how professionals evaluate their potential use remains limited. This study reports an exploratory mixed-method case evaluation of a generative AI–based demonstrator that translates legal and policy text together with geospatial inputs into a machine-readable spatial artefact, illustrated through a wind-energy opportunity-mapping case for the Province of Utrecht. Methods The evaluation combined a qualitative expert comparison with an existing professionally produced reference map, two purposively composed expert focus groups, descriptive Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) questionnaires, a public-values ranking, and reflexive thematic analysis. Value Sensitive Design (VSD) was used as an empirical and interpretive lens to identify public and professional values relevant to further development of the demonstrator and underlying workflow. Results The reference comparison showed that the demonstrator could generate a structurally recognizable spatial output, but also revealed crucial discrepancies, including missing buffers, insufficient differentiation of constraint categories, and weak grounding of some policy-based constraints. Questionnaire and focus-group findings indicate that participants recognized potential usefulness, particularly for rapid exploration and synthesis, while simultaneously emphasizing the need for validation, traceability, controllability, and human oversight. Discussion Given the small expert samples and exploratory design, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of professional technology adoption. The evaluated demonstrator should instead be understood as an exploratory proof of concept whose outputs are not yet sufficiently reliable for authoritative spatial-planning use. Quantitative spatial validation, reproducibility testing, and stronger integration of deterministic validation mechanisms remain necessary next steps.

documents.abstract: Generative AI chatbots have become part of 15-year-olds' schoolwork. However, it is less clear whether these students also evaluate what these systems produce. Using PISA 2025 data from more than 500,000 students across 59 countries, we examined how often students are asked in class to evaluate AI output, who is asked, and how closely the practice is associated with students' AI use. On average across countries, 57.5% of students used AI chatbots for schoolwork at least weekly, yet only 35.3% reported being asked often or very often to evaluate the quality of AI output in class, whereas 33.2% reported being asked never or almost never. Interestingly, students who used AI more often also reported being asked more often to evaluate AI output, in all countries (pooled r = 0.34). Yet, 25% of at-least-weekly users still reported no or almost no AI-output evaluation. Furthermore, students from more advantaged socioeconomic backgrounds reported being asked more often to evaluate AI output, independent of their level of AI use. Overall, students reported being asked to evaluate AI output less often than to evaluate online information. Yet, the association of AI use with evaluation was substantially stronger for AI-output than for online-information evaluation. In sum, many students who use AI regularly report few opportunities to evaluate its output in lessons, and these opportunities are socially stratified, extending an established pattern of digital inequality to generative AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Passenger trust plays a critical role in the adoption of autonomous vehicles (AVs), especially in complex traffic environments where system behavior may be difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a framework linking driving characteristics (e.g., acceleration profiles, responsiveness to other road users, maneuvering patterns) with passengers’ emotional responses and perceived safety. The framework examines how adaptive, emotion-aware human–machine interfaces (HMIs) can enhance transparency and comfort by responding to real-time user states such as stress or discomfort. It combines biometric data (e.g., heart rate variability, skin conductance) with self-reported feedback to assess passenger experience in realistic scenarios, with particular emphasis on in-vehicle cues and external indicators contributing to perceived trust. The approach builds on insights from European research projects, including SHOW, AUGMENTED CCAM, DIVERSITY, DIVERSIFY CCAM, DRIVE2theFuture, AWARE2ALL, and ULTIMO, and aligns conceptually with the Horizon Europe project CERTAIN. Rather than presenting experimental results, the paper proposes a conceptual framework and outlines a methodological pathway for its future empirical validation in driving simulation or controlled automated vehicle environments.

AbstractArtificial intelligence [AI] encompasses advanced computational system designed to execute functions that normally depend on human cognitive abilities, such as learning inference problem solving, and decision-making Therapeutic progress in information systems, the expansion of big data and the growth in computing resources have generally facilitated the incorporation of AI into pharmaceutical and health care sectors. This technological integration has promoted strong partnerships between pharma organizations and AI solution providers , learning to a transformation in technical drug development approaches.AI technologies are now applied across various phases pf pharmaceutical research and development, including identification of therapeutic targets, discovery of new drug molecules, formulation development, designing dosage forms, optimization of clinical manufacturing processes, quality management and quality control , and regulatory submissions . In addition, AI facilitates drug repositioning, accelerate research activities, and automates routine process which collectively enhances productivity, accuracy, and efficiency while reducing both time and operational costs. nevertheless, the practical adoption of AI is accompanied by several barriers, including concerns related to data integrity and availability, complex regulatory requirements, ethical and privacy issues, the limited explainability of AI algorithms, and the shortage of trained professionals with domain expertise. This review aims to explore the contribution of artificial intelligence, particularly artificial neural networks and other AI- based approaches, in pharmaceutical development. It also focuses on the key benefits, existing challenges, and future opportunities, providing insights into how AI can further drive innovation and efficiency in the pharmaceutical industry.Keywords AI, Pharmaceutical Sciences, learning inference problem solving, and decision-making Therapeutic progress.

documents.abstract: This study examined acceptance-related perceptions of ChatGPT among first-year engineering students at a Chilean university. Psychometric analyses included 206 respondents completing all 32 items; inferential analyses included 178 reporting study-related use. Drawing on an extended technology acceptance model as a descriptive framework, we analyzed perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived intelligence, perceived trust, awareness, and adoption intention in relation to gender, school sector, prior academic performance, and usage frequency. Internal consistency estimates were high, but exploratory factor analysis showed incomplete separation of the dimensions, limiting claims of construct validity. After Holm correction, no comparisons by gender, school sector, or prior academic performance remained statistically significant. More frequent use was associated with higher scores across all six dimensions. The findings provide preliminary psychometric evidence and identify usage frequency as the most consistent correlate of acceptance-related perceptions. However, the cross-sectional design does not permit conclusions about directionality, causality, or educational benefits.

European air traffic management (ATM) is facing increasing delays and capacity challenges, necessitating new approaches to automation and human-AI collaboration. This paper examines the SESAR exploratory research projects AISA (AI Situational Awareness Foundation for Advancing Automation) and its continuation, AWARE (Achieving Human-Machine Collaboration with Artificial Situational Awareness), through the lens of Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs). AISA introduced the concept of AI-based situational awareness using knowledge graphs and reasoning engines, while AWARE advances this work with an AI assistant that monitors air traffic controllers’ intent, workload, and interaction to provide tailored support. Although officially classified at low TRL levels, both projects developed and validated components reaching higher maturity, reflecting the need for demonstrable solutions even in early research. The analysis highlights the potential of human-AI teaming to increase safety, capacity, and efficiency in ATM, while emphasising the importance of gradual, validated integration of AI into this safety-critical domain.
topics: Military Command and Control and Network-Centric Warfare

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI), is transforming tourism-related tasks and creating new competency requirements for future professionals. This conceptual paper synthesises research on AI competencies and contextualises them within tourism occupations. It proposes the Tourism AI Competency Framework, comprising six domains: (1) AI literacy; (2) AI application in tourism; (3) data and analytical literacy; (4) digital customer experience; (5) human–AI collaboration; and (6) responsible AI use. The framework comprises three developmental levels, progressing from awareness to application and AI-augmented professional practice. The paper argues that AI integration should not be reduced to the addition of a standalone technology course. Instead, curriculum redesign should begin with changes in occupational tasks and translate these changes into competencies, learning outcomes, learning activities, and assessment.
